No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I mean, things are heavy, but I don't want to disappear. Disappearing just sounds... complicated. 

Like those magicians on TV, you know? The ones who make whole monuments vanish. David Copperfield did the Statue of Liberty back in the 80s. I remember watching that special with my dad. We had this big, clunky Zenith television set with the faux-wood paneling on the sides. My dad was convinced the whole Statue of Liberty thing was just a camera trick with mirrors. He was a mechanic, so he always tried to figure out the mechanics of everything. No, not really sad. It's not sadness, it's just... I don't know, empty? Like I'm just going through the motions. 

It's sort of like when you're watching a movie and the audio gets out of sync with the picture. Yeah, that's actually the main reason I finally came in to see you. The things that usually make me feel like myself... they just feel completely flat and heavy now. Like my photography walks. I used to go out every weekend with my camera, just looking for interesting light or architecture.

Well, no, not two years. Like I was saying before, it's really been about a year and three months of this. It all started right after my sister's health got bad and her behavior got so unpredictable, and I had to step in and take over coordinating everything for her. 

Speaking of coordinating, I actually had to call her insurance company three times this week just to get a prior authorization for a new medication. The hold music they play is just awful, it's this really tinny, repetitive jazz loop that sounds like it was recorded underwater. I'm exactly the same size I've always been.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in most things most of the time?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I mean... it's like I was saying before, it's pretty much everything. I just don't care about much of anything right now. It's like someone turned the volume down on my whole life. \n\nIt reminds me of when my old stereo receiver finally gave out. The volume knob just completely stopped working. I'd turn it and turn it, and nothing would happen, just this faint little hum from the speakers. I bought that stereo at a garage sale back when I was taking classes at the community college. The guy who sold it to me was this retired mechanic who had an entire garage full of vintage audio equipment. He had these huge floor speakers that must have weighed a hundred pounds each. He told me he used to build custom sound systems for classic cars in the seventies. My dad had a '72 Chevelle, actually. It was this metallic forest green color. He spent every Sunday morning waxing that car in the driveway. He'd use these special microfiber cloths he ordered from a catalog, and he wouldn't let anyone else touch the paint. One time, the neighbor's kid accidentally hit a baseball into the side panel and left a tiny dent, and my dad didn't speak to the neighbor for like six months. It was so awkward because they shared a property line and had to mow right next to each other...\n\nBut, uh, sorry. Yeah. Most things, most of the time. Just completely lost interest.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel sad most of the time?\n\nPatient: No, not really sad. It's not sadness, it's just... I don't know, empty? Like I'm just going through the motions. \n\nIt's sort of like when you're watching a movie and the audio gets out of sync with the picture. You're seeing people's mouths move, but the words don't match up, and it just takes you completely out of the story. I was trying to watch this documentary the other night about the history of the postal service, and the streaming app kept glitching out like that. It was fascinating, though, learning about how they used to deliver mail on horseback, the Pony Express and all that. Imagine having to ride a horse across the country just to deliver a letter. Horses are such beautiful animals, but they kind of intimidate me. They're so big, and they have those massive teeth. My cousin went horseback riding on her honeymoon in Costa Rica and she got thrown off and broke her collarbone. She had to wear this special brace for weeks, and it totally ruined the rest of their trip. They were supposed to go zip-lining through the rainforest, which sounds amazing, but also terrifying. I don't know if I could trust a little metal wire to hold me up hundreds of feet in the air. \n\nBut, um, yeah. No, I wouldn't say I feel sad. Just... not much of anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from activities that you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Yeah, that's actually the main reason I finally came in to see you. The things that usually make me feel like myself... they just feel completely flat and heavy now. Like my photography walks. I used to go out every weekend with my camera, just looking for interesting light or architecture. \n\nI have this old Nikon, a manual film camera that I bought from a pawn shop downtown. The guy who ran the shop was this real character, always smoking a cigar inside, which I'm pretty sure is illegal now. He had all these antique pocket watches in a glass case, and he told me he used to repair them himself. Pocket watches are so intricate, you know? All those tiny little gears and springs. It makes you wonder how anyone ever had the patience to put them together by hand. I tried to fix a wristwatch once, just a cheap digital one where the battery died, and I ended up losing one of those microscopic screws in the carpet. I vacuumed the entire living room twice trying to find it, but it was just gone. Vacuums are so loud, though. My upstairs neighbor runs hers at like six in the morning on Saturdays, and it sounds like a jet engine taking off right above my bed. I've thought about leaving a note on her door, but I don't want to start any drama. I have to see her in the laundry room sometimes, and she always uses way too much fabric softener. The whole basement smells like artificial lavender for days after she does her wash...\n\nBut, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, the photography walks, mentoring the kids at the community center, even just keeping my work calendar organized... I just stopped initiating any of it. It all just feels too heavy.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if your feelings of heaviness and lack of interest have been consistent over the past 15 months, or have they varied in intensity?\n\nPatient: Yeah, it's been pretty consistent. Like, a year and three months of this. It all really started after my sister's health started going downhill and her behavior got so erratic, and I had to step in and take on all the coordination for her care. \n\nIt's a lot of coordination, honestly. You wouldn't believe the amount of paperwork involved in just getting someone a home health aide. It's like buying a house, the stacks of forms you have to sign. When I bought my condo, the closing took three hours because the printer at the title company kept jamming. It was this massive industrial printer, one of those ones that takes up a whole corner of the room, and the guy kept having to open all these different little doors on it to pull out shredded pieces of paper. I used to work in an office where we had a printer like that, and there was this one guy, Gary, who was the only one who knew how to fix it. Gary was obsessed with model trains. He had this entire setup in his basement, like a whole miniature town with tiny streetlights that actually worked and little plastic people waiting at the station. He showed me pictures once at the company holiday party. Those parties were always so strange, standing around eating lukewarm Swedish meatballs with people you usually only email. I always ended up talking to the accounting department because they were the only ones who didn't want to talk about work...\n\nBut, um, sorry. Yeah. About fifteen months. It's been heavy like this the whole time since I had to start managing everything for her.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have days where you feel more interested in things than others, or is it the same level of disinterest all the time?\n\nPatient: Well, there are definitely times when it's not the same level. Like, if someone just moves a meeting on my calendar by 15 minutes, or changes a small detail, I get incredibly sharp with them. Nobody knows how to use it properly. It's supposed to color-code everything automatically, but it keeps making all my one-on-ones this awful neon green color. Neon green reminds me of those glow sticks we used to get at the roller rink when I was a kid. Did you ever go roller skating? I loved the couples skate, even though I was terrible at it and always ended up holding onto the wall. The rink had this snack bar that sold the best soft pretzels, the kind that are practically dripping with butter and those big chunks of salt. I tried to make soft pretzels at home once during the pandemic when everyone was baking bread, but the dough didn't rise right. I think my yeast was dead. It's so weird that yeast is a living thing, isn't it? Just this fungus that makes bread fluffy. I watched a whole video on YouTube about how sourdough starter is basically just capturing wild yeast from the air. Some people have starters that are like a hundred years old, passed down through generations. Imagine inheriting a jar of fermented flour from your great-grandmother...\n\nBut yeah, um, what was I... oh, the interest. So it's not always just flat disinterest. Sometimes I get really upbeat and sure of everything, but then I get surprisingly snappy over tiny things.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever have periods where your interest in activities returns to normal, or is it always diminished?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not exactly that it goes back to a normal, relaxed kind of interest. He used it to label all these glass baby food jars he kept his screws and washers in. He had the metal lids nailed to the underside of this wooden shelf, so you just had to twist the jar to take it down. It was genius, honestly. You don't really see glass baby food jars much anymore, do you? Everything is in those little plastic squeezy pouches now. My cousin's toddler eats mashed sweet potatoes out of those pouches, and she always manages to get orange puree all over their upholstery. They have this cream-colored sofa, which is just a terrible idea if you have kids or pets. I don't know why anyone buys white furniture, you're just asking to be stressed out every time someone sits down with a cup of coffee...\n\nBut, um, anyway. What I was saying is, during those stretches, I'm just doing all of it at the same time. The templates, the emails, the filing. It just feels like sitting still would mean I'm dropping the ball.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt this way for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not two years. We had this bulky CRT television in our dorm room, the kind that weighed like eighty pounds, and we'd sit up until three in the morning trying to beat these impossible levels. My roommate, Greg, was incredibly good at it. He ended up dropping out to start a landscaping business, which is funny because he was allergic to grass. He had to wear these special masks and long sleeves in the middle of summer just to mow a lawn. I wonder what he's up to now. Probably still sneezing...\n\nBut, um, yeah. Not two years. Just the last fifteen months or so, since I took on all her stuff.\n\nDoctor: Is your lack of interest in activities something that you experience all the time, or are there periods where it improves?\n\nPatient: Well, it's pretty constant, honestly. The morning light has this incredible golden quality to it, right around 6:30 AM. Photographers call it the 'golden hour,' though technically there's one in the evening too.
